results.derivation_summary: Under 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2)(i), a debt collector is presumed to comply with the prohibition on harassing repeated calls (and FDCPA § 806(5)) if it places calls to a particular person about a particular debt neither more than seven times in seven consecutive days, nor within seven consecutive days after having had a telephone conversation with that person about that debt (the conversation date counts as day one). Exceeding either frequency creates a presumption of violation under § 1006.14(b)(2)(ii). The limits run per 'particular debt' — each debt in collection is counted separately (except student loans serviced under one account number, which count as one debt) — and calls that are placed with the person's prior consent within seven days of that consent, that do not connect to the dialed number, or that go to persons listed in § 1006.6(d)(1)(ii)–(vi) do not count toward the frequencies under § 1006.14(b)(3).

edge_cases.scenario: Within 30 days of receiving the validation notice, the consumer mails the collector a written dispute demanding verification of the debt. The collector never mails verification but keeps calling her 4 times a week about the same account.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node has no screen for a timely written dispute/verification request under 15 U.S.C. 1692g(b) (and 12 CFR 1006.34/1006.38), which requires the collector to CEASE collection activity -- including collection calls -- until verification is mailed. Four calls a week is under the ceiling with no conversation, so the encoded logic outputs 'presumptively compliant.' The checklist captures only a 1692c(c) written cease-communication notice or a written refusal to pay, and treats 'I do not owe this' merely as a rebuttal factor; a validation request is neither, yet it independently bars the calls. The consumer would be told her strongest, cleanest claim does not exist.

edge_cases.scenario: The consumer filed a Chapter 7 petition (or received her discharge) three weeks ago; the collector, notified or not, continues calling her about the pre-petition credit-card debt three times a week.
edge_cases.gap_description: Nothing in the logic or checklist screens for a pending bankruptcy or discharge. Three calls a week with no conversation yields 'presumptively compliant,' but the calls violate the automatic stay (11 U.S.C. 362(a)(6)) or the discharge injunction (11 U.S.C. 524(a)(2)), carrying contempt sanctions and actual/punitive damages, and typically also 1692c(a)(2) (debtor represented by bankruptcy counsel) and 1692e(2). The node's whole design is to warn that 'presumptively compliant' does not clear independent bars (1692c(a), (c), 1692b/c(b), state law); the single most consequential independent bar for a frequently-called consumer is missing.

edge_cases.scenario: The same charged-off account is worked by two entities in the same week -- e.g., the debt buyer's in-house collectors call 6 times Monday-Wednesday and the outside agency it just placed the file with calls 6 times Thursday-Saturday -- so the consumer reports 12 calls about one debt in seven days.
edge_cases.gap_description: unit_of_count is stated as 'per particular PERSON and per particular debt' only; it never says the count is also per DEBT COLLECTOR, and the determination triggers on 'call_count_in_trailing_7_days > 7 for the same debt AND same recipient.' 12 CFR 1006.14(b)(2) measures calls 'a debt collector' places, so each collector has its own bucket. Applied as encoded, the node reports presumptive violations where, as against each collector individually, none exists -- overstating the consumer's claim and misdirecting it at the wrong defendant (the correct theory here is the rebuttable 1006.14(a)/1692d(5) aggregate-harassment analysis, not the 7-in-7 presumption). The checklist's 'from this collector' phrasing is the only thing partially guarding against this and it is not carried into the operative rule.

results.derivation_summary: Under 15 U.S.C. § 1692a(6), a person is a 'debt collector' if the principal purpose of its business is collecting debts, or if it regularly collects (directly or indirectly) debts 'owed or due or asserted to be owed or due another,' subject to exclusions for creditor employees, affiliated collectors, government officers, process servers, nonprofit credit counselors, and persons collecting debts that they originated, that were not in default when obtained, or that arise from fiduciary/escrow or secured commercial-credit arrangements. A 'creditor' under § 1692a(4) is one who extends credit or is owed the debt (excluding one who takes assignment of a defaulted debt solely to collect for another), and a 'debt' under § 1692a(5) is a consumer obligation to pay money arising from a transaction primarily for personal, family, or household purposes — so business-purpose obligations fall outside coverage. Henson holds that a firm collecting debts it purchased for its own account is not covered by the 'owed another' prong (leaving the 'principal purpose' prong unresolved), and Obduskey holds that an entity doing no more than nonjudicial foreclosure/security-interest enforcement is a debt collector only for purposes of § 1692f(6). For the communication rules, 'consumer' is expanded by § 1692c(d) and 12 C.F.R. § 1006.6(a) to include the spouse, parent of a minor, guardian, executor/administrator, and (under Regulation F) a confirmed successor in interest.

results.derivation_summary: Under the FDCPA, a 'debt collector' is a person whose principal business is collecting debts or who regularly collects debts owed to another. The law applies only to 'debts' incurred by a consumer for personal, family, or household purposes. A creditor collecting its own debt, or a company that buys debt to collect for its own account, is generally not considered a 'debt collector' under the statute's primary definition.

semantic_agreement_judge.agreement_notes: All three agree on the core definitions: 'debt collector' covers principal-purpose or regular collection of debts owed another, 'debt' is limited to consumer obligations for personal/family/household purposes, and a creditor or debt buyer collecting for its own account generally falls outside the 'owed another' prong (Henson). Completeness differences only: Analysis 3 omits Obduskey's § 1692f(6) carve-out, the statutory exclusions, and the § 1692c(d)/Regulation F expanded 'consumer' definition, and it does not flag that Henson left the 'principal purpose' prong open — nuances Analyses 1 and 2 supply without contradicting it.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer gets dunning letters and calls that appear entirely in her original credit card issuer's name and branding, but the letters are actually generated and the calls actually placed by an outsourced third-party collection vendor the issuer hired to work delinquent accounts under the issuer's brand. The consumer answers the gate's first question by describing the entity as 'the bank, in its own name.'
edge_cases.gap_description: Checklist item 1 and determination step (1) are framed around the NAME appearing on the communication rather than the identity of the actor. Exclusion (A) reaches only an officer or employee of the creditor; a separate hired vendor collecting debts owed to another is a covered debt collector even when it collects entirely in the creditor's name (and may separately implicate 1692j flat-rating). As encoded, brand-name outsourcing -- extremely common in card, auto, and utility collections -- is dispositively routed to 'excluded,' writing off a real claim.

results.derivation_summary: Under Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a), an action on any contract, obligation, or liability founded upon a written instrument must be brought within four years (with a special three-month rule for deficiency money judgments after a trustee's/mortgage power-of-sale sale). Once that four-year period has run, § 337(d) prohibits filing suit, arbitration, or any other legal proceeding to collect the debt, and the period can be extended only under § 360 — i.e., by a signed written acknowledgment or promise, or by a payment of principal or interest, though no payment can revive a claim already barred. Additional text supplies tolling/adjustment rules that can affect the count: emergency rule 9(a) tolled limitations periods exceeding 180 days from April 6, 2020 to October 1, 2020; 50 U.S.C. § 3936(a) excludes a servicemember's period of military service; 11 U.S.C. § 108(c) extends a period that had not expired at a bankruptcy filing to at least 30 days after the stay ends; and § 361 bars suits already time-barred where the cause of action arose out of state.
results.citation_used: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337(a) (four-year period), with § 337(d) and § 360 (extension/revival limits)

semantic_agreement_judge.agreement_notes: All three agree the limitations period on a written contract/debt is four years (Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 337), that after it runs suit or other collection proceedings are barred, and that extension requires a signed written acknowledgment or promise under § 360. diagnostics.manual_verification_note: Two independent reasons the live checker cannot verify this entry mechanically: (1) the previous url (www4.courts.ca.gov/documents/appendix-i.pdf) returns HTTP 403 to the checker on every run since 2026-09-02; (2) the rule exists only as a PDF and the checker has no PDF text extractor, so no courts.ca.gov url will ever substring-match. Url moved to the Judicial Council's own amendment order (courts.ca.gov/system/files/rules-court/20-05-28-rules-effective-20-05-29.pdf, 'Amendments to the California Rules of Court, adopted by the Judicial Council on May 28, 2020, effective May 29, 2020'), fetched and read in full 2026-09-04: rule 9(a) as amended reads 'Notwithstanding any other law, the statutes of limitations and repose for civil causes of action that exceed 180 days are tolled from April 6, 2020, until October 1, 2020.' (the PDF is a redline that also shows the struck original end-date language); 9(b) tolls periods of 180 days or less until August 3, 2020; the Advisory Committee Comment confirms the rule reaches limitations periods in codes other than the CCP. Confirmation by Claude (Cowork); not yet independently re-confirmed by Andy.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer's mother died in 2023 owing a 2021-defaulted Chase card balance; the debt buyer sues the estate (or the daughter as successor) in 2026. The node computes accrual 2021 + 4 years (+ possible tolling) and reports the claim as still live/about to expire.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node has no screening question for a deceased debtor. CCP § 366.2 imposes a one-year-from-death outer limit on any cause of action that survives against a decedent, which overrides the otherwise-applicable 4-year contract period and is not subject to most tolling. Here the correct answer is that the claim was barred in 2024, but the node would tell the heir/estate the debt is still enforceable — a materially wrong answer in the direction that costs the family money. Decedent-debt inquiries are a routine slice of consumer-debt practice (collectors regularly dun estates and surviving relatives).

edge_cases.scenario: A debt buyer sues on a Capital One card; the consumer says 'they can never produce a signed contract — I never signed anything.' Applying the checklist's written-vs-oral classification item, the analysis routes the matter to the 2-year oral-contract node and reports the 2022-default debt as time-barred in 2026.
edge_cases.gap_description: The written/oral binary omits the third and, for revolving accounts, controlling alternative: a credit-card balance is pleadable as an open book account or account stated under CCP § 337(b)/(a), both carrying 4 years, so the 2-year oral period is essentially never the operative floor for card debt even when no signed cardmember agreement exists. The node mentions § 337(b) only in passing inside the revival note as 'not encoded here.' A consumer told the suit is time-barred may simply not answer, and — as this node's own affirmative-defense caveat warns — take a default judgment on a live claim.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer who moved to California from Texas is served with an application to enter a sister-state judgment (CCP § 1710.10 et seq.) based on a 2013 Texas default judgment on a card debt, on which no execution ever issued. The judgment_enforcement_note tells them any entered judgment is 'enforceable for 10 years from entry, renewable without limit' under CCP § 683.020.
edge_cases.gap_description: CCP § 683.020 governs California judgments; enforcement of an out-of-state judgment turns first on whether the judgment remains enforceable under the rendering state's law (Texas judgments become dormant after 10 years without execution and must be revived), and an independent California action on a sister-state judgment is separately governed by CCP § 337.5(b). The node's flat 10-year/renewable statement can wrongly tell a consumer an unrevivable foreign judgment is enforceable (or, in a 20-year state, that it has lapsed). Interstate moves plus debt-buyer domestication filings make this a recurring California fact pattern that the checklist never asks about.
